locator: section 4, The ORDER BY clause, first paragraph
claim: SQLite states that a SELECT returning more than one row without ORDER BY has an undefined row order.
quote: If a SELECT statement that returns more than one row does not have an ORDER BY clause, the order in which the rows are returned is undefined.

locator: LIMIT Clause, paragraph beginning "When using LIMIT"
claim: PostgreSQL advises using an ORDER BY clause that makes the order unique when using LIMIT, because otherwise the returned subset of rows is unpredictable.
quote: When using LIMIT, it is a good idea to use an ORDER BY clause that constrains the result rows into a unique order. Otherwise you will get an unpredictable subset of the query's rows — you might be asking for the tenth through twentieth rows, but tenth through twentieth in what ordering?

locator: section 4, The ORDER BY clause, paragraph beginning "Rows are first sorted"
claim: SQLite sorts by the leftmost ORDER BY expression and breaks ties with later expressions; rows equal on every ordering expression are returned in an undefined order.
quote: Rows are first sorted based on the results of evaluating the left-most expression in the ORDER BY list, then ties are broken by evaluating the second left-most expression and so on. The order in which two rows for which all ORDER BY expressions evaluate to equal values are returned is undefined.

locator: ORDER BY Clause, paragraph beginning "The ORDER BY clause causes"
claim: PostgreSQL compares tied rows by the next ORDER BY expression and returns rows equal on all specified expressions in an implementation-dependent order.
quote: The ORDER BY clause causes the result rows to be sorted according to the specified expression(s). If two rows are equal according to the leftmost expression, they are compared according to the next expression and so on. If they are equal according to all specified expressions, they are returned in an implementation-dependent order.

locator: section 4, The ORDER BY clause, paragraph beginning "SQLite considers NULL values"
claim: SQLite treats NULL as smaller than every other value, so NULLs appear first in ascending order and last in descending order by default, and explicit NULLS LAST/FIRST syntax can change this.
quote: SQLite considers NULL values to be smaller than any other values for sorting purposes. Hence, NULLs naturally appear at the beginning of an ASC order-by and at the end of a DESC order-by. This can be changed using the "ASC NULLS LAST" or "DESC NULLS FIRST" syntax.

locator: ORDER BY Clause, paragraph beginning "If NULLS LAST is specified"
claim: PostgreSQL defaults to NULLS LAST for ascending order and NULLS FIRST for descending order, as though nulls were larger than non-nulls, and accepts explicit NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST.
quote: If NULLS LAST is specified, null values sort after all non-null values; if NULLS FIRST is specified, null values sort before all non-null values. If neither is specified, the default behavior is NULLS LAST when ASC is specified or implied, and NULLS FIRST when DESC is specified (thus, the default is to act as though nulls are larger than non-nulls).

locator: section 7, Collating Sequences, BINARY bullet; section 7.1 states the default
claim: SQLite's BINARY collation compares string data using memcmp, regardless of text encoding.
quote: BINARY - Compares string data using memcmp(), regardless of text encoding.

claim: PostgreSQL gives a column reference the column's defined collation, a constant its data type's default collation, and a more complex expression a collation derived from its inputs.
quote: If the expression is a column reference, the collation of the expression is the defined collation of the column. If the expression is a constant, the collation is the default collation of the data type of the constant. The collation of a more complex expression is derived from the collations of its inputs, as described below.

locator: section 2.2, Date and Time Datatype, first paragraph
claim: SQLite has no dedicated date/time storage class; its built-in date and time functions store dates and times as TEXT, REAL, or INTEGER, with the TEXT form being an ISO-8601 string.
quote: SQLite does not have a storage class set aside for storing dates and/or times. Instead, the built-in Date And Time Functions of SQLite are capable of storing dates and times as TEXT, REAL, or INTEGER values: - TEXT as ISO8601 strings ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.SSS").

claim: RFC 3339 says strings with components ordered from least to most precise, the same time-zone spelling, and the same number of fractional-second digits may be sorted as strings.
quote: If date and time components are ordered from least precise to most precise, then a useful property is achieved. Assuming that the time zones of the dates and times are the same (e.g., all in UTC), expressed using the same string (e.g., all "Z" or all "+00:00"), and all times have the same number of fractional second digits, then the date and time strings may be sorted as strings

locator: section 8.5.1.3, Time Stamps, paragraph beginning "In a value that has been determined"
claim: For timestamp without time zone, PostgreSQL ignores any time zone indication and keeps the input's date and time fields without adjusting them for a zone.
quote: In a value that has been determined to be timestamp without time zone, PostgreSQL will silently ignore any time zone indication. That is, the resulting value is derived from the date/time fields in the input string, and is not adjusted for time zone.

locator: section 8.5.1.3, Time Stamps, paragraph beginning "For timestamp with time zone values"
claim: For timestamp with time zone, an input without a stated zone is assumed to be in the session TimeZone and converted to UTC; in either case PostgreSQL stores UTC and does not retain the original stated or assumed zone.
quote: If no time zone is stated in the input string, then it is assumed to be in the time zone indicated by the system's TimeZone parameter, and is converted to UTC using the offset for the timezone zone. In either case, the value is stored internally as UTC, and the originally stated or assumed time zone is not retained.
